extracted.intended_audience: advertisers, marketers, advertising agencies, and their legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for advertisers on what makes disclosures effective and lawful across media, and standards for nutrient, health, and efficacy claims for foods, drugs, devices, and dietary supplements under FTC (and FDA-linked) enforcement. Covers requirements for print, TV, and Internet disclosures and specific rules tied to FDA definitions and statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: whether the qualifying information is prominent enough for consumers to notice and read (or hear)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prominence is a core factor the Commission considers when evaluating the effectiveness of disclosures; disclosures that are not noticeable to consumers fail this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: whether the qualifying information is presented in easy-to-understand language that does not contradict other things said in the ad and is presented at a time when consumers’ attention is not distracted elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentation requires clear, non-contradictory language and timing that ensures consumers can process the disclosure rather than being distracted by other ad elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement
rubrics_metrics.description: whether the qualifying information is located in a place and conveyed in a format that consumers will read (or hear)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement must position the disclosure where consumers actually see or hear it (formatting and location matter); e.g., buried fine print often fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: whether the qualifying information is located in close proximity to the claim being qualified
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosures should appear near the claim they modify so consumers can easily connect the qualification to the relevant claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and conspicuous standard
rubrics_metrics.description: disclosures must be 'clear and conspicuous' — generally readable (or audible) and understandable to a reasonable consumer
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission reiterates the clear-and-conspicuous standard in workshops and policy statements; in cases the standard has been defined as 'readable [or audible] and understandable to a reasonable consumer.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Print-disclosure adequacy (avoid reliance on fine print)
rubrics_metrics.description: fine-print footnotes or blocks of text in print ads and point-of-sale materials are frequently inadequate to disclaim or modify a claim made elsewhere in the promotion
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative cases challenge use of inconspicuous or unreadable fine print to disclose material information (e.g., fuel fees, limitations on 'free' offers); print disclosures must be prominent, legible, and proximate to the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television-disclosure effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: video superscripts that are difficult to understand, superimposed over distracting backgrounds, compete with audio elements, or are placed in parts of the ad less likely to be remembered have been found to be ineffective in modifying a claim made in the body of the ad
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TV disclosures must be legible, contrasted against backgrounds, timed and located so they do not compete with audio or other ad elements; complicated superscripts or text that can't be read in context will not cure deceptive claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet-disclosure clarity and conspicuousness
rubrics_metrics.description: online disclosures must meet the same clarity and conspicuousness principles; guidance exists on how FTC law applies online with a focus on clarity and conspicuousness of online disclosures
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FTC staff paper 'Dot Com Disclosures' and subsequent letters (e.g., to search engines) provide guidance on labeling paid placements and ensuring online disclosures are visible, understandable, and not hidden by design or links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of FDA-approved nutrient and health claims on labels
rubrics_metrics.description: only FDA-approved nutrient content and health claims may appear on labels under the Nutrition Labeling and Education Act (NLEA)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing label claims the Commission defers to FDA-approved terms and claims; non-approved claims on labels can violate both FTC and FDA regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute nutrient content claims must follow FDA definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: the Commission will apply FDA’s definitions for terms such as low fat and high fiber
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marketers using absolute nutrient-content terminology must ensure those terms match FDA regulatory definitions to avoid deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serving size standard
rubrics_metrics.description: the Commission will use FDA’s serving sizes in analyzing nutrient content claims
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims based on serving size should be evaluated using FDA-prescribed serving sizes to ensure accuracy and prevent misleading per-serving statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative/comparative nutrient-content claims
rubrics_metrics.description: unqualified comparative claims must meet FDA’s minimum percentage difference requirements; other comparative claims that are accurately qualified to identify the nature of the increase or reduction and to eliminate misleading implications may also comply
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative claims must either meet FDA numeric thresholds or be clearly and accurately qualified so consumers are not misled about the magnitude or meaning of the comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synonyms consistency with FDA definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: claims that characterize the level of a nutrient, including those using synonyms not provided for in FDA’s regulations, must be consistent with FDA definitions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using alternate wording (synonyms) for regulated nutrient terms is permissible only if the synonyms convey the same meaning as FDA-defined terms so consumers are not misled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health-claim substantiation and qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: the Commission will use FDA’s 'significant scientific agreement' standard as its principal guide in determining whether unqualified health claims are substantiated; health claims that are not yet FDA-approved must be adequately qualified so that consumers understand both the extent of the support for the claim and any significant contrary evidence
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unqualified health claims must meet the high scientific-agreement standard; provisional or emerging claims require clear qualifiers and disclosure of contrary evidence and often require disclosure of risk-increasing nutrients to avoid deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 15 definitions for 'drug' claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 15 of the FTC Act defines 'drug' to include articles intended 'for use in the diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment, or prevention of disease' or intended 'to affect the structure or any function of the body.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because this statutory definition encompasses therapeutic claims, efficacy claims about products that meet the definition are subject to heightened scrutiny and must be substantiated; the Commission has challenged unsubstantiated drug claims in numerous cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 15 definitions for 'device' claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 15 of the FTC Act defines 'device' to include 'instruments, apparatus, and contrivances' intended 'for use in the diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment, or prevention of disease' or intended 'to affect the structure or any function of the body.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efficacy and safety claims about devices that fall within this definition require substantiation; the Commission has pursued enforcement against deceptive device claims (examples include pain-relief bracelets, home test kits, and other medical-device claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact Lens Rule: prescription release and verification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: the Contact Lens Rule imposed new prescription release and verification requirements on prescribers and sellers pursuant to the Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act of 2003
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission enforces requirements such as prescribers' obligation to release prescriptions to patients and prohibitions on conditioning prescription release on purchase or charging additional fees; staff sent warning letters to alleged violators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dietary-supplement advertising: basic advertising-law principles apply
rubrics_metrics.description: the Commission's Dietary Supplements: An Advertising Guide for Industry describes how the basic principles of advertising law apply to the marketing of dietary supplements
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplements cannot be advertised with unsubstantiated disease-treatment or efficacy claims; the FTC enforces through law enforcement, industry outreach, and education and has brought many cases challenging deceptive supplement claims (including requirements for disclosures and, in some cases, safety/interactions warnings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to disclose material risks or interactions when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: in many cases, the presence and significance of risk-increasing nutrients or safety interactions must be disclosed to prevent a health claim from being deceptive
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include requiring warnings about St. John's Wort interactions or other safety disclosures when a product's promotion could otherwise mislead about safety or suitability for certain consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on unsubstantiated disease-treatment or cure claims for foods, supplements, and devices
rubrics_metrics.description: representations that products can treat, prevent, or cure serious diseases without adequate substantiation are deceptive and have been subject to enforcement actions and civil penalties
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The document lists many representative cases where claims that supplements, foods, devices, or other products could treat or cure diseases (e.g., cancer, AIDS, diabetes) led to consent orders, large redress amounts, and other penalties.
